question: Following the Supreme Court's judgment in Common Cause v Union of India (2018), which statement correctly describes the legal position on euthanasia in India?

answers.text: Both active and passive euthanasia are legal in India, provided the patient has executed a valid Advance Directive.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Active euthanasia (lethal act by a doctor) remains illegal in India — it constitutes culpable homicide under the IPC. Only passive euthanasia is legalised under the 2018 ruling.

answers.text: Passive euthanasia — withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment — is legal in India under a valid Advance Directive or through the structured safeguard procedure in Common Cause 2018.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The Supreme Court in Common Cause (2018) held that passive euthanasia is constitutional, recognising the right to die with dignity under Article 21. Advance Directives are valid; a structured procedure applies when no directive exists.

answers.text: Euthanasia of all forms remains illegal; the Aruna Shanbaug (2011) judgment remains the final word.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The Aruna Shanbaug judgment (2011) permitted passive euthanasia in specific circumstances. Common Cause (2018) went further — it recognised the right to die with dignity and made Advance Directives legally valid.

answers.text: Active euthanasia is legal when requested by the patient's next of kin and approved by two independent physicians.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Active euthanasia is not legal in India under any circumstances. No mechanism — family request or medical endorsement — legalises a lethal act.

overallFeedback.feedback: Active euthanasia is illegal in India. Passive euthanasia is legal (withdrawal of treatment) — established by Common Cause v Union of India (2018), building on Aruna Shanbaug (2011).
Correct. Common Cause (2018): passive euthanasia legal + Advance Directives valid. Active euthanasia remains illegal (IPC culpable homicide). Aruna Shanbaug (2011) was the earlier precedent.
